impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims reciting a genus of antibodies (anti-CGRP antagonist humanized monoclonal antibodies) for treating headache, where any member of the genus would be effective for the claimed treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines Amgen v. Sanofi enablement standards by sustaining overly broad genus claims for method patents. The decision preserves broad patent protection for biologic drug methods despite concerns about overbreadth.
impacts.positiveImplications: Biopharmaceutical patent holders benefit from broader enablement standards for method claims, allowing genus-level claims covering classes of antibodies to withstand invalidity challenges, thereby strengthening patent portfolios and market exclusivity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor drug developers and biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially limiting freedom to operate and increasing licensing costs for antibody-based treatments.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award for misappropriation of proprietary automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating it. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from the reinstatement of jury damages awards and broader consideration of damages methodologies, strengthening enforcement of contractual and trade secret protections in technology licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology licensees face increased exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims when developing replacement software after license expiration, with potentially broader damages theories available to plaintiffs on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to enforcement-only operations triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling it to sue in its own name without joining the university. The court also held that shifting to enforcement-only activities did not constitute ceasing business operations under the agreement's termination clause.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent enforcement entities benefit from clarified standards for standing, confirming that comprehensive exclusive licenses can convey sufficient rights to maintain infringement suits independently, and that enforcement-focused business models do not automatically trigger license termination.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on standing challenges to exclusive licensees, and patent owners may find it harder to regain control over enforcement when licenses are drafted broadly.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The split ruling on eligibility across related patents provides important guidance on Alice step-two analysis for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications and digital signal processing benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for implementation-specific claims and the preservation of a substantial damages verdict, reinforcing that applied technical improvements can survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued infringement exposure, and the vacatur of eligibility for certain claims creates uncertainty about the scope of patent protection for constellation mapping innovations.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield different results and specifies conditions inconsistent with the referenced testing standard.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of the '287 patent are invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could yield materially different results depending on which testing method and conditions were used. The specification identified multiple methods (upright, inverted, Mocon) and specified conditions (40°C, 20% humidity) that conflicted with the ASTM E96-94 standard it referenced, leaving skilled artisans without reasonable certainty about claim scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and textile industries benefit from strengthened indefiniteness doctrine when patent claims reference measurable properties without adequately specifying the measurement protocol.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming functional performance ranges in materials patents must ensure their specifications clearly identify a single, reproducible testing methodology, or risk invalidation for indefiniteness.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims to a communications apparatus reciting a transformer with a 'non-magnetic core' for matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness finding but affirmed final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the patent's claims, which required transmitting signals 'over air' using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match impedance, were not enabled because the specification did not teach how to achieve the claimed impedance matching across the full scope of the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached below, providing efficiency in patent litigation. The ruling reinforces that enablement requires the specification to teach the full scope of claimed functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face heightened risk that claims will be invalidated on enablement grounds even when indefiniteness challenges fail, particularly for claims reciting broad functional results without adequate specification support.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification discloses preparation methods and characterization data for the claimed crystalline forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description for claims to crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate, an active ingredient in the cancer drug Cabometyx®. The decision upholds key patents protecting a blockbuster oncology drug against generic entry, with the patents terminally disclaimed to expire in 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from confirmation that crystalline form patents with disclosed preparation methods and characterization data satisfy written description, protecting drug products from generic competition through patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the validity of key formulation patents is upheld, delaying access to lower-cost alternatives.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder filed suit despite PTO rejections of related claims under § 101 and abandonment of related applications.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of fee-shifting and sanctions motions, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a plaintiff that filed an infringement suit after Alice despite PTO § 101 rejections of closely related patent claims, raising concerns about exceptional case determinations under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's requirement that district courts provide detailed reasoning when denying fee motions, increasing the likelihood that meritless patent assertions will result in fee awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting when bringing infringement claims where closely related patents or applications have been rejected on eligibility grounds, as courts must now more rigorously explain denials of fee requests.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims directed to oil and gas well float tools, and whether the resulting infringement and validity determinations were correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment on infringement and validity of claims in the '445 patent relating to oil and gas casing float tools. The case involves claim construction disputes over structural terms in mechanical patents used in the energy industry, with significant implications for competing wellbore completion products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas industry benefit from the Federal Circuit's careful scrutiny of claim construction, potentially broadening the scope of protection for wellbore completion tool patents on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the oilfield services market face continued uncertainty about the scope of float tool patents, with remand potentially resulting in broader infringement findings.

impacts.caseName: Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce properly used the invoice date rather than an alternative date as the 'date of sale' for calculating antidumping duty rates on Turkish steel rebar imports under 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed Commerce's use of the invoice date as the date of sale for antidumping duty calculations on Turkish steel rebar, upholding the regulatory presumption under 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i). The decision reinforces Commerce's discretion in selecting the date of sale methodology in antidumping proceedings, affecting how duty rates are calculated for imported steel products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers benefit from the affirmation of Commerce's methodology, which supports antidumping duty orders protecting U.S. steel markets from below-normal-value imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel exporters face limited ability to challenge Commerce's default use of invoice dates in antidumping calculations, potentially resulting in higher duty rates when material terms of sale are established before invoicing.
